title: What is Bootstrap?
summary: Introduces Bootstrap as a pre-made CSS framework (2010, from two Twitter developers), weighs its pros and cons, and shows how to add it through a CDN link. A short exercise has the learner add the stylesheet, drop in a Bootstrap card, point its image at a local file and centre it with an override style using Flexbox.

concepts.heading: What Bootstrap is
points: A CSS framework: a ready-made stylesheet (and optional script) you include in a project and then use by adding class names to your HTML.

Created in 2010 by two Twitter developers, Mark Otto and Jacob Thornton. It is open source, so its CSS can be browsed on GitHub (for example the card component defines classes for card body, title, subtitle and so on).
A plain HTML button looks basic; adding about five Bootstrap classes turns it into a styled button. You only need to know which classes to use, not write the CSS.
A major reason for its popularity is the 12-column layout system built on Flexbox, designed for responsive, mobile-first sites that look right on phones and desktops.

Other frameworks: Foundation, MUI, Tailwind and more. Bootstrap holds the largest share among frameworks (roughly 80% of framework users in the figures shown), but the biggest group of sites uses no framework at all.
Bootstrap does not replace Flexbox, Grid or float knowledge. Learned CSS stays relevant, and you should be able to build without a framework.

concepts.heading: Pros and cons of CSS frameworks
points: Pros: quick and easy to use; many ready components (pricing plans, cards, navbars); consistent styling across a site; good cross-browser compatibility already tested for you.
Con: class bloat. Styling lives in the HTML class attributes, which blurs the usual rule of HTML for structure and CSS for style, and markup gets cluttered.
Con: customisation. If every pixel must follow a custom design, overriding each component is time consuming.
Good fit: a mobile-first responsive site that must go online fast and look polished and uniform. Poor fit: a very simple page, or a complex bespoke design needing total control.

concepts.heading: Adding Bootstrap with a CDN
points: A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a set of servers around the world that serves a file from a location near the visitor, so the Bootstrap CSS downloads quickly.
Copy the stylesheet link from getbootstrap.com and put it in the head. It is an ordinary link element with rel="stylesheet" whose href points at the CDN file.
The .min in the filename means minified: whitespace removed so the file is smaller and loads faster. It is unreadable for humans but works the same.
For interactive features (dropdowns, collapsing menus, and similar), include Bootstrap's script tag just before the closing body tag. This lesson only needs the CSS.
(Extra) The copied link also contains integrity and crossorigin attributes. integrity is a hash the browser checks so a tampered file is rejected.

concepts.heading: Overriding Bootstrap styles
points: To change a Bootstrap style, your rule must win: use an internal style element, an inline style, or an external stylesheet linked after the Bootstrap link, because later rules override earlier ones of equal specificity.
Your CSS can build on Bootstrap's rules or define properties Bootstrap never touches.
In the exercise the card wrapper has a custom class, flex-container, styled by you (not part of Bootstrap).

pitfalls: Leaving the card image src as the docs placeholder, so the image looks broken.
Linking your own stylesheet before Bootstrap so your overrides lose.
Forgetting height: 100vh, so vertical centring has no effect.
Treating the framework as a replacement for CSS knowledge.
(Extra) The reference repo uses a different Bootstrap version between index.html (5.3.3) and solution.html (5.3.0-alpha2), and each page has a personal footer line to ignore.
